subject: BFA8DCA4C0C24066BAF0F869C88CF522
introduction: These readings hold two things together. Creation was called 'out of utter nothingness' by the will of God and depends on Him at every moment; and creation has no beginning in time, for a Creator without a creation is not conceivable. They resolve this by distinguishing what is eternal in essence from what is eternal only in time and preceded by a cause, and they read the six days and the six thousand years of scripture as figures. Each of the thirty-two quotations is read here beside one from elsewhere. Most stand alongside: 'Let there be light', the Qur'an's 'Be! and it is', the Word of John's Gospel, Plato, Plotinus, Aquinas, the Upanishad, Augustine on time, the Gita's ages. Four push back or add a side: Genesis says that the work was finished, the Qur'an counts six days, Heraclitus has an eternal world with no maker, and the Rig Veda doubts that anyone knows.
questions: The readings say both that creation came from nothingness and that it never had a beginning. How does the distinction between pre-existence in essence and in time hold the two together?
'There can be no creator without a creation.' What does that argument assume about God, and do you find it persuasive?
Genesis and the Qur'an speak of six days and a finished work. What is gained and what is risked in reading them as having an inner meaning?
Heraclitus's world is eternal and unmade; the readings' creation is eternal and dependent. What difference does dependence make to how a person lives?

outside.why: The letter to the Hebrews says that the worlds were framed by the word of God, so that things which are seen were not made of things which do appear.
Plotinus says that the One, seeking nothing and lacking nothing, has overflowed, and its exuberance has produced the new.

Heraclitus also held that the world had no beginning: it was ever, is now, and ever shall be an ever-living Fire, and no god made it. What is the difference between an eternal world without a maker and an eternal creation?

Genesis says that the heavens and the earth were finished, and that God ended his work and rested on the seventh day. How do the readings understand a text that seems to give creation a beginning and a completion?
Jesus says, when blamed for healing on the sabbath: my Father worketh hitherto, and I work.
The psalmist considers the heavens, the moon and the stars, and asks what man is, that God is mindful of him.
The Revelation has the Lord say: I am Alpha and Omega, the beginning and the ending, which is, and which was, and which is to come.
Malachi has God say in five words what the reading says at length: I am the Lord, I change not.
Isaiah has God say: I am the first, and I am the last, and beside me there is no God.
The Qur'an says that His command, when He intendeth a thing, is only that He saith unto it: Be! and it is.
Genesis tells the first act of creation in a sentence: and God said, Let there be light: and there was light.
John's Gospel opens: in the beginning was the Word, and all things were made by him.
Genesis says that God formed man of the dust of the ground, and breathed into his nostrils the breath of life.
Plato distinguishes that which always is and has no becoming from that which is always becoming and never is.
Lucretius held, as the first principle of his account of nature, that nothing from nothing ever yet was born.
Aquinas argued that it is necessary to admit a first efficient cause, to which everyone gives the name of God.
The Chandogya Upanishad asks how that which is could be born of that which is not, and answers: only that which is, was in the beginning.
Origen asked who of understanding will suppose that the first days of creation, with evening and morning, existed without a sun.
Peter's letter says that one day is with the Lord as a thousand years, and a thousand years as one day.
The Rig Veda's hymn of creation ends by asking who verily knows whence this creation came. What is the right tone for speaking of a station that 'can never be described nor even alluded to'?
Moses asks God what he shall say to the children of Israel when they ask who has sent him.
The psalm says that by the word of the Lord were the heavens made, and all the host of them by the breath of his mouth.
The Qur'an says that God created the heavens and the earth in six days. If creation has no beginning from which to reckon, what are the six days telling?
The Qur'an says of God: vision comprehendeth Him not, but He comprehendeth all vision.
The Qur'an calls God the Originator of the heavens and the earth, who saith unto a thing only: Be! and it is.
The psalm says that the heavens shall wax old like a garment and be changed, but thou art the same.
Krishna says in the Gita that at the close of each age all things return into his being, and at its beginning issue new-born from him.
Lamentations says that the Lord's compassions fail not; they are new every morning.
In the same book Augustine asks what time is, and says that he knows until someone asks him to explain.
Plato calls time a moving image of eternity, made together with the heaven.
Paul speaks of God, who quickeneth the dead, and calleth those things which be not as though they were.
The Tao Teh King says that all things sprang from it as existing, and that existence sprang from it as non-existent.
